summary: Golden, airy yeast-risen dough balls fried until crisp outside and cloud-soft within, lightly sweet and dusted with sugar if you like.
story: Puff puff is one of Nigeria's most common fried snacks, sold at roadsides and served at weddings, birthdays and other celebrations. It is simple street food that nearly everyone has a family way of making, with some cooks adding nutmeg, pepper or a little more sugar.

items.name: Warm water
items.note: around 38°C, comfortably warm to the touch

steps.title: Mix the batter
steps.text: Whisk the flour, sugar, yeast, salt and nutmeg in a large bowl. Pour in most of the warm water and beat with your hand or a wooden spoon for 2 to 3 minutes. The batter should be thick, stretchy and fall off the spoon in a slow ribbon, thicker than pancake batter. Add the remaining water only if it feels stiff.

steps.title: Let it rise
steps.text: Cover the bowl with a clean cloth and leave it somewhere warm for 45 to 60 minutes. It is ready when it has doubled, the surface is bubbly and it smells pleasantly yeasty.

steps.title: Stir down briefly
steps.text: Give the batter one or two gentle stirs to knock out the biggest bubbles but keep it airy. Do not beat it again or the puffs will turn dense.

steps.title: Heat the oil
steps.text: Pour the oil into a deep pot to a depth of about 6 cm and heat to 170 to 175°C. Test with a small drop of batter: it should sink briefly, then rise and sizzle steadily within a few seconds.

steps.title: Shape and fry
steps.text: Scoop batter in your fist and squeeze it out between thumb and forefinger, or use two oiled spoons, to drop walnut-sized balls into the oil. Fry 5 to 6 at a time so the temperature stays steady. They will puff and roll over on their own.

steps.title: Turn until golden
steps.text: Keep turning the puffs every minute or so for 4 to 6 minutes in total. They are done when deep golden brown all over and sound hollow when tapped. Break one open to check there is no raw dough inside.

steps.title: Drain and serve
steps.text: Lift out with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels or a wire rack. Roll in sugar while still warm if you wish, and eat the same day, preferably within the hour.

tips: Oil that is too hot browns the outside before the centre cooks; too cool and the puffs soak up oil and go greasy. Adjust the heat between batches.
Do not over-ferment the batter. If it smells sharply sour, the puffs will taste sour.
A slightly wet, sticky batter gives the lightest puffs. A stiff dough makes dense ones.
Use a thermometer if you have one; otherwise rely on the drop test.

swaps.swap: Use 1 tbsp active dry yeast dissolved in the warm water with a pinch of sugar for 10 minutes first. Rise time is similar.
Ground cinnamon or a pinch of ground ginger gives a different but pleasant warmth.

name: Puff Puff
